name: Pale Umber
lede: Pale Umber is ColorHub's English name for Rikyū-nezumi, a greyish olive that the traditional Japanese color list ties to the tea master Sen no Rikyū, prized for its understated, tea-ceremony restraint.

sections.title: A tea master's grey-green
sections.body:
Wikipedia's list of traditional Japanese colors gives this swatch as Rikyū-nezumi (利休鼠), named for the sixteenth-century tea master Sen no Rikyū and nezumi ("mouse"), marking it as a muted grey-green favored in the understated aesthetic he championed [1]. ColorHub's English rendering, Pale Umber, reaches for a pigment word rather than naming the tea master [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 places the swatch in block 113, "olive gray," about 5.1 units from that block's centre [2]. The library's nearest other named color is [[bronzesheen]], 2.8 units away [2].

Measured in LCH it reads lightness 42, chroma 8, hue 100 degrees, a mid-dark, barely saturated olive [2]. The name's tea-ceremony restraint and the measured low chroma point the same way: a deliberately subdued color, not a vivid one [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match in 3,251 of 23,781 paintings, about 14 percent, as photographed [3]. It plays a mid-tone role most often, 57 percent of its occurrences, with highlight and shadow splitting the rest [3]. Johan Jongkind and Frederic Remington each carry it at more than three and a half times the archive's overall rate [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with the color words Grey, Gunmetal and [[taupe]], and its presence peaks around the 1270s, in early Chinese bamboo paintings [3].
